title: Systematic Dishonesty: Manipulated Tests, a Complicit Testing House, and a Department That Was Well Aware

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving was the price difference between combustible and fire-resistant product, taken by selling the cheaper one into a market told it was safe. The Inquiry finds Celotex "embarked on a dishonest scheme to mislead its customers and the wider market" in order "to break into the market for insulation suitable for use on high-rise buildings, created and then dominated by Kingspan K15"; and that Kingspan "knowingly created a false market in insulation for use on buildings over 18 metres in height".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was in the test, and it was physical. In May 2014 Celotex tested a system "that contained two sets of fire-resistant magnesium oxide boards placed in critical positions to ensure that it passed", then obtained a report "that omitted any reference to the magnesium oxide boards, thereby rendering it materially incomplete and misleading". The Inquiry finds the Building Research Establishment "was complicit in that strategy", and separately that senior BRE staff "gave advice to customers such as Kingspan and Celotex on the best way to satisfy the criteria for a system to be considered safe, thereby compromising its integrity and independence".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was manufactured and sustained for more than a decade. From early 2005 Arconic held test data showing Reynobond 55 PE in cassette form "reacted to fire in a very dangerous way and could not be classified in accordance with European standards", yet "persisted in telling the market that the panels had been classed B-s2, d0 without drawing any distinction between the cassette and riveted forms", and "deliberately concealed from the market the true extent of the danger" until after the fire. The Inquiry's summary of the whole class of conduct: "systematic dishonesty on the part of those who made and sold the rainscreen cladding panels and insulation products ... deliberate and sustained strategies to manipulate the testing processes, misrepresent test data and mislead the market".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was market access that honest testing would have denied, protected by the certificates that were supposed to police it. The certification bodies, the British Board of Agrément and Local Authority Building Control, "failed to ensure that the statements in their product certificates were accurate and based on test evidence", and UKAS, "the body charged with oversight of the certification bodies, failed to apply proper standards of monitoring and supervision". By summer 2011 Arconic "was determined to exploit what it saw as weak regulatory regimes in certain countries (including the UK)" to keep selling the cassette form for residential buildings.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment ran for twenty-six years and it was inaction rather than an inquiry. "In the years between the fire at Knowsley Heights in 1991 and the fire at Grenfell Tower in 2017 there were many opportunities for the government to identify the risks ... Indeed, by 2016 the department was well aware of those risks, but failed to act on what it knew." It had been warned in terms: the Inquiry records the department's failure "to heed the warning of the Environment and Transport Select Committee in December 1999 that it should not take a serious fire in which people were killed before steps were taken to minimise the risks posed by some external cladding systems."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A building-safety regime resting on manufacturer-commissioned testing, third-party certification of the resulting claims, and statutory guidance that the department had been advised for years was inadequate.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Inquiry's findings and recommendations, and the post-Grenfell reconstruction of building regulation around a single regulator — arriving, as the Inquiry notes of the 1999 warning, only after the fire in which people were killed.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The manipulated test produced the certificate; the certificate satisfied the specifier; the specification created the market; and the testing house that could have broken the loop was advising the manufacturers on how to pass. The department that might have changed the rule had been told what would happen if it did not.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Grenfell was a council's cost-cutting on one refurbishment — a cheap cladding choice by a landlord — or, alternatively, that it was an unforeseeable combination that no regulation could have anticipated.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Inquiry locates the cause well upstream of the refurbishment and well before 2017. Its conclusion is that the fire "was the culmination of decades of failure by central government and other bodies in positions of responsibility in the construction industry", that "by 2016 the department was well aware of those risks, but failed to act on what it knew", and that a select committee had warned in December 1999 against waiting for a fatal fire. And the products were not innocently misunderstood: the Inquiry finds "systematic dishonesty" by the manufacturers, a test manipulated with concealed magnesium oxide boards, a test report rendered "materially incomplete and misleading", and a testing house "complicit in that strategy". What the Inquiry does not do is determine liability: it is a statutory inquiry making findings of fact and recommendations, and criminal investigations remained separate from it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A finding of systematic dishonesty by the makers of the cladding panels and insulation, consisting of deliberate and sustained strategies to manipulate testing, misrepresent test data and mislead the market. A May 2014 BS 8414 test of Celotex RS5000 containing two sets of fire-resistant magnesium oxide boards placed to ensure a pass, and a resulting report omitting any mention of them. BRE found complicit in that strategy, and found to have advised Kingspan and Celotex how to satisfy the safety criteria while certifying them. Arconic holding test data from early 2005 on the cassette form's fire behaviour, telling the market the panels were B-s2, d0 without distinguishing the forms, and deliberately concealing the danger until after the fire. Kingspan knowingly creating a false market for use above 18 metres. Certification bodies failing to ensure their certificates were accurate and evidence-based, and UKAS failing to supervise them. And a department that, by 2016, was well aware of the risks and failed to act on what it knew.

citations.title: Grenfell Tower Inquiry: Phase 2 Report (Sir Martin Moore-Bick, chairman; Ali Akbor OBE and Thouria Istephan, panel), Volume 1, HC 19-I, presented to Parliament under section 26 of the Inquiries Act 2005, ordered printed 4 September 2024
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the UK government's own asset store and read as extracted text. NOTE ON ACCESS: the Inquiry's own site, grenfelltowerinquiry.org.uk, now redirects to the National Archives web archive, which serves a human-verification challenge; that challenge was not circumvented, and the report was taken from the government publishing host instead. THE OVERALL CONCLUSION, at paragraph 2.4: "We conclude that the fire at Grenfell Tower was the culmination of decades of failure by central government and other bodies in positions of responsibility in the construction industry to look carefully into the danger of incorporating combustible materials into the external walls of high-rise residential buildings and to act on the information available to them." ON GOVERNMENT, at 2.5: "In the years between the fire at Knowsley Heights in 1991 and the fire at Grenfell Tower in 2017 there were many opportunities for the government to identify the risks posed by the use of combustible cladding panels and insulation, particularly to high-rise buildings, and to take action in relation to them. Indeed, by 2016 the department was well aware of those risks, but failed to act on what it knew. In particular, it failed to heed the warning of the Environment and Transport Select Committee in December 1999 that it should not take a serious fire in which people were killed before steps were taken to minimise the risks posed by some external cladding systems." ON THE MANUFACTURERS, at 2.19: "One very significant reason why Grenfell Tower came to be clad in combustible materials was systematic dishonesty on the part of those who made and sold the rainscreen cladding panels and insulation products. They engaged in deliberate and sustained strategies to manipulate the testing processes, misrepresent test data and mislead the market. In the case of the principal insulation product used on Grenfell Tower, Celotex RS5000, the Building Research Establishment (BRE) was complicit in that strategy." At 2.20 the Inquiry finds that the certification bodies, the British Board of Agrément and Local Authority Building Control, "failed to ensure that the statements in their product certificates were accurate and based on test evidence", and that "UKAS, the body charged with oversight of the certification bodies, failed to apply proper standards of monitoring and supervision." ON THE TESTING HOUSE, at 2.18: there were weaknesses in BRE's conduct of BS 8414 tests and in its record-keeping "which exposed it to the risk of manipulation by unscrupulous product manufacturers, as happened in the case of the second test carried out for Celotex", and "Senior BRE staff gave advice to customers such as Kingspan and Celotex on the best way to satisfy the criteria for a system to be considered safe, thereby compromising its integrity and independence." ON THE INDIVIDUAL MANUFACTURERS: Arconic, from 2005 until after the fire, "deliberately concealed from the market the true extent of the danger of using Reynobond 55 PE in cassette form, particularly on high-rise buildings", having held test data from early 2005 showing the cassette form "reacted to fire in a very dangerous way and could not be classified in accordance with European standards", yet "persisted in telling the market that the panels had been classed B-s2, d0 without drawing any distinction between the cassette and riveted forms"; by summer 2011 "it was well aware" of the difference and "was determined to exploit what it saw as weak regulatory regimes in certain countries (including the UK)". Celotex "embarked on a dishonest scheme to mislead its customers and the wider market": in May 2014, "With the complicity of BRE", it tested a system "that contained two sets of fire-resistant magnesium oxide boards placed in critical positions to ensure that it passed", then obtained a test report "that omitted any reference to the magnesium oxide boards, thereby rendering it materially incomplete and misleading", and marketed the product on that test without disclosing the manipulation. Kingspan, "From 2005 until after this Inquiry had begun ... knowingly created a false market in insulation for use on buildings over 18 metres in height", a claim that was false "as it well knew". A statutory public inquiry: it makes findings of fact and recommendations and determines no civil or criminal liability.
